panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 3 panels (A, B, C). A: Clinical photo of a child's mouth showing the classic Riga-Fede combination of lower natal teeth and a ventral tongue ulcer, directly supported by the caption and article title. B: Intraoral radiograph demonstrates the natal teeth that are the predisposing manifestation in Riga-Fede disease, as stated in the caption. C: Gross specimen of extracted natal teeth from the patient, supporting the natal-teeth component of Riga-Fede disease; no ulcer is visible in this panel.

panels.rationale: Single clinical photograph of an infant/child oral cavity showing a large ulcer on the ventral tongue and two mandibular primary central incisors. The caption explicitly identifies Riga-Fede disease and describes the ulcer and teeth. This is a real patient image with no third-party copyright or annotations.
panels.attribution_text: Dairo et al. Management of Severe Riga-Fede Disease in a Child With MIRAGE Syndrome.. Cureus 2025. doi:10.7759/cureus.97970. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 1.
panels.figure_caption: Initial dental consult exam revealed Riga-Fede disease A 16 mm X 8 mm ulceration on the ventral surface of the tongue and the two erupted mandibular primary central incisors were noted.
in_text_mentions: y was significant for premature birth, pancytopenia, and massive intracranial hemorrhage within days of birth. A comprehensive workup ultimately revealed a diagnosis of MIRAGE. The intraoral examination revealed two incisors in the anterior mandible and an ulceration on the ventral surface of the tongue (Figure 1). Further examination of the oral ulceration revealed a rectangular lesion estimated to be 16 mm by 8 mm in contact with the mandibular central incisors. No other lesions were appreciated on the intraoral mucosa. Based on the history and clinical features, a diagnosis of RFD was made.

panels.figure_caption: Indurated, non-tender, ulcerative swelling on the ventral surface of the tongue measuring 1.5 by 1.5 cm. Impressions of the primary lower central incisors were seen in the middle of the lesion.
in_text_mentions: Physical examination revealed an indurated, non-tender, ulcerative swelling on the ventral surface of the tongue measuring 1.5 by 1.5 cm. Impressions of the primary lower central incisors were seen in the middle of the lesion (Figure 1). On palpation, the lesion seemed to infiltrate deep into the underlying muscle. A close relationship between the tumor and the primary lower central incisors was noticed during swallowing.

panels.rationale: Single clinical photograph of a one-month-old infant showing two natal teeth and an ulcerated lesion on the ventral surface of the tongue, the classic manifestation of Riga-Fede disease. The panel is a real patient image and the caption/in-text directly support the diagnosis.
panels.attribution_text: Volpato et al. Riga-Fede Disease Associated with Natal Teeth: Two Different Approaches in the Same Case.. Case reports in dentistry 2015. doi:10.1155/2015/234961. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 1.
panels.figure_caption: One-month-old infant showing the presence of two natal teeth in the lower arch and ulcerated lesion in the ventral surface of the tongue.
in_text_mentions: Intraoral examination revealed two natal teeth in the mandibular anterior region and an ulcerated lesion on the ventral surface of the tongue (Figure 1). The lesion had a diameter of 8 mm and was located at the midline anterior portion of the ventral surface of the tongue and seemed to have the impression of the teeth on its center due to repetitive trauma resulting from raking movements of the tongue against the anterior natal teeth leading to the clinical diagnosis of Riga-Fede Disease.

panels.rationale: Single-panel haematoxylin-eosin micrograph (10x) of the excisional biopsy from a newborn with traumatic lingual ulceration; the caption and in-text statement describe an ulcerative inflammatory lesion with granulation tissue and a mixed infiltrate including abundant eosinophils, and the authors base the diagnosis of Riga-Fede disease on these clinicopathological findings. Histology of granulation tissue at the ulcer base is a recognized histological correlate of Riga-Fede disease, though the infiltrate itself is non-specific, hence moderate confidence.
panels.attribution_text: van der Meij et al. Traumatic lingual ulceration in a newborn: Riga-Fede disease.. Italian journal of pediatrics 2012. doi:10.1186/1824-7288-38-20. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 2.
panels.figure_caption: Mixed cellular infiltrate consisting of lymphocytes, neutrophils, plasma cells, and an abundant number of eosinophils (haematoxylin-eosin, 10x).
in_text_mentions: Excisional biopsy was performed under general anesthesia. The resulting defect was closed primarily. On histopathological examination an ulcerative, inflammatory lesion with granulation tissue was seen. The mixed cellular infiltrate consisted of lymphocytes, neutrophils, plasma cells, and an abundant number of eosinophils (Figure 2). Based on the clinicopathological findings a diagnosis of Riga Fede disease was made.

The article title and in-text mention of extraction support disease attribution, though the caption does not explicitly name the manifestation.

in_text_mentions: obility (Class 3), so the tooth was extracted during the first portion of surgery to prevent interference with otolaryngology’s procedure. A single mandibular occlusal radiograph was obtained (Figure 7). A flap was raised to uncover and access #N (lower left primary lateral incisor) for extraction. #P (lower right primary central incisor) was extracted.
